content_voiceover: This table on the staging of iron deficiency is extremely high-yield. Stage 1, prelatent, is pure storage depletion: bone marrow iron is reduced, ferritin falls, TIBC rises, but serum iron, transferrin saturation, hemoglobin, and MCV are all still normal — no anemia yet, usually asymptomatic. Stage 2, latent or iron-deficient erythropoiesis: marrow iron is now absent, ferritin drops under 30, serum iron and transferrin saturation fall below 16%, soluble transferrin receptor and free erythrocyte or zinc protoporphyrin rise, and reticulocyte hemoglobin content falls — but hemoglobin and MCV are still normal, though the patient may report fatigue and malaise. Only in stage 3 does frank anemia appear: hemoglobin and MCV finally drop, and you see classic symptoms — pallor, pica, epithelial changes like koilonychia or glossitis. The teaching point: ferritin and reticulocyte hemoglobin content are abnormal well before hemoglobin drops, so iron studies catch deficiency before anemia develops. On the right, etiology: dietary deficiency alone takes about eight years to cause IDA in an adult, so if you diagnose IDA in an adult, you must actively search for another cause — decreased intake or absorption, such as gastric surgery, celiac disease, or elevated hepcidin from inflammation or TMPRSS6 mutation; increased loss, with GI bleeding and occult malignancy being the most dangerous to miss, alongside menorrhagia; or increased requirement, as in pregnancy and infancy.
keypoints: Stage 1 (prelatent): ferritin ↓, TIBC ↑ — everything else still normal
Stage 2 (latent): TSAT <16%, sTfR ↑, retic Hb content ↓ — Hb/MCV still normal
Stage 3 (anemia): Hb ↓, MCV ↓, symptomatic (pallor, pica, glossitis)
Diet alone takes ~8 years to cause IDA in adults — always hunt for a cause
Top causes: GI bleed/malignancy, malabsorption, menorrhagia, increased demand
keypoint_voiceover: Iron deficiency progresses through three stages. Stage 1 is storage depletion only, ferritin down, TIBC up, but hemoglobin normal. Stage 2 adds iron-deficient erythropoiesis, transferrin saturation under 16%, soluble transferrin receptor up, but still normal hemoglobin. Only stage 3 is true anemia with low hemoglobin and MCV. Since diet alone takes about 8 years to cause IDA, any adult with iron deficiency anemia needs a workup for the cause — think GI bleeding and malignancy first, then malabsorption or increased demand.
